conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Dr. Miller, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re adjusting to life with your new baby and to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Today I’ll be using the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, and any thoughts of self-harm that can pop up in the first year after birth. It’s just 10 questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days; your answers are confidential and will help me figure out the best next steps for your care.

We’ll keep the room quiet and judgment-free, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[eyes a little watery, gives a half-shrug]

Honestly… most of the time it feels kind of forced. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I managed a little chuckle, but it faded fast. Nothing really feels funny these days—everything just seems heavy, like I’m too tired or worried to find much humor in anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

Not really… I mean, I can smile if someone shows me something cute the baby does, but it’s like the laughter gets stuck. I’ll try to laugh along when my partner jokes, but it feels hollow—like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[glances down at hands]

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but this week even the idea of meeting up feels exhausting. I still go, because I know I “should,” but I’m not really looking forward to anything. It’s like the color’s drained out of it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[voice drops, eyes well up]

Yeah… pretty often. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I didn’t swaddle him right, or I ate the wrong thing, or I’m just not soothing him the way a “good mom” would. Later I found myself apologizing to my partner for the house being messy, even though he said it’s fine. I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilty feeling just sits there.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings a burp cloth in her lap]

Almost every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s breathing too fast, or I’ll lie down at night and picture him spitting up and choking when I’m asleep. Nothing’s actually happened, but the thoughts just pop in and won’t leave. Sometimes I have to get up three or four times to check the monitor even though I know he’s fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods, voice shaky]

Yes… it’s like a sudden wave, especially in the evenings. My chest gets tight, my heart starts pounding, and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. There’s no real reason—just this dread that something awful is about to happen, like I’m failing him or that I’ll never feel normal again. It usually passes after a while, but it’s scary when it hits.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly]

Yes… most days. Between the night feedings, the piles of laundry, and trying to remember if I even ate lunch, it feels like I’m drowning a little. I’ll start one task and get interrupted by a cry or a diaper blow-out, and by dinnertime nothing’s finished and I’m just… done. I keep telling myself I should be able to handle it, but it keeps piling up anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[bites lip, eyes rimmed red]

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop. I replay every little thing—did I sterilize the bottles right, why didn’t he smile today, am I already ruining him—and then I’m wide-awake. Some nights I drift off okay, but I jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t get back to sleep for an hour or two. It’s like the sadness just keeps circling while the house is quiet.
I have felt sad or miserable

[presses a crumpled tissue against her eyes]

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. Even when the baby gives me a little smile, the happiness feels… short-lived. I’ll be folding his tiny clothes and just start crying because everything feels so heavy and lonely.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, throat tight]

Yes… it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I burst into tears while trying to make a sandwich—couldn’t even say why. The smallest thing sets me off, and once I start I can’t seem to stop. I feel silly afterward, but in the moment it just pours out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he needs.

You've shared how the color seems to have drained out of life since your baby arrived: laughter feels hollow, outings feel like chores, and a gray cloud of sadness follows you most days. Despite putting on a brave face, you're battling waves of worry about your son's safety, intense panicky surges at night, and a relentless sense that you're somehow failing as a mom. You cry easily, feel guilty over everyday hiccups, and lie awake replaying every detail. Still, you're clear that you want to be here for your baby and simply wish to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes markedly reduced ability to laugh, with laughter feeling "hollow" and "stuck," aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports inability to anticipate enjoyment from previously pleasurable activities, indicating "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>She reports blaming herself "pretty often" and gives two specific recent examples, aligning with "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive, daily worries about infant safety with physical anxiety symptoms and compulsive checking behaviors</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, breathlessness) occurring "quite a lot" without clear triggers</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('most days'), multiple stressors, and inability to complete tasks, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries preventing sleep onset plus middle-of-the-night waking, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent daily sadness, feeling followed by a "gray cloud," crying spells, and inability to feel lasting joy even with infant smiles.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, uncontrollable crying episodes triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. You endorse <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most days, plus <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>impaired concentration</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance linked to mood</sym>, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Co-occurring <med>anxiety symptoms</med> (panic episodes, compulsive checking) are also prominent. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss formal evaluation and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>, and whether an <med>antidepressant</med> might help
3. Reach out today to a trusted adult who can stay with you and the baby while you seek care; share your EPDS score so they understand the urgency
4. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress once treatment begins
5. Practice brief self-compassion exercises when guilt surfaces-remind yourself "I am learning and my baby needs me, not perfection"
6. Aim for one 15-minute block of rest daily while a support person watches the baby; adequate rest modestly improves mood and anxiety
7. Keep a simple log of feedings and mood to identify patterns to review with your provider
8. Maintain current safety plan: continue to voice any scary thoughts immediately to a support person or clinician
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Patient: Postpartum adult (spontaneous report)

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Daily low mood, frequent crying (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (Q3)  
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious thoughts and nocturnal panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and functional impairment (Q6)  
- Insomnia linked to ruminative worry/sadness (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present "most days this week," interfere with enjoyment of infant and tasks of daily living.  
Sleep disturbance is mood-related rather than solely infant-driven.

Risk factors noted:
- Persistent sadness, loss of pleasure  
- Guilt/feelings of inadequacy as mother  
- Anxiety/panic without clear trigger  
- Overwhelm and coping difficulty  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood

Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10); no protective-concern flags voiced.

Screening significance: Clinical picture consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in the postpartum period; possibility of comorbid anxiety disorder. Recommend completion of validated postpartum depression measure (e.g., EPDS) and prompt follow-up with obstetric/primary or behavioral health for formal evaluation and treatment planning.
